headline: Fruit is bribery—tasty packages that convince animals to spread seeds
universal_truth: Getting others to help often requires giving them something they want
fun_facts: Many fruits are designed to pass through animal digestive systems—seeds germinate better after being eaten
Some fruits evolved to be eaten by dinosaurs; after extinction, new animals took over seed-spreading duties
The avocado was likely spread by giant ground sloths; today humans are its main dispersers
discussion_questions: Why would a plant 'want' its seeds eaten?
What happens to a fruit after an animal eats it?

hook.script: Why do apples taste good? Not for you—for the tree. Fruit is a bribe: 'Eat me, carry my seeds somewhere else.' The sweetness is payment for transportation. Plants can't walk, so they recruit animals to move their offspring.

cliff.script: Being eaten seems like a bad strategy for survival. Why would plants wrap their seeds in something delicious that gets consumed?
cliff.prompt: Why do plants make tasty fruit around their seeds?

options.text: Animals eat the fruit, travel somewhere, and deposit seeds in their droppings—free transportation and fertilizer
options.response: Yes. The seed survives digestion, travels with the animal, and gets deposited with ready-made fertilizer. It's a transportation deal.

options.text: The sweet fruit protects seeds from rotting before they can grow
options.response: Protection helps, but the main purpose is convincing animals to carry seeds away...

fact1.title: Seed Taxis
fact1.script: A seed falling beneath its parent competes with that parent. Plants benefit when seeds travel far. Fruit recruits animal taxis—birds, mammals, even fish—to carry seeds miles from home. Distance equals opportunity.

fact2.title: Digestive Benefits
fact2.script: Many seeds germinate better after passing through digestive systems. Stomach acid weakens the seed coat. Droppings provide fertilizer. Being eaten isn't just tolerated—it's often beneficial to the seed.

fact3.title: Lost Partners
fact3.script: The avocado evolved to be eaten by giant ground sloths—now extinct. Its large seed was meant for large digesters. Today, only humans regularly spread avocado seeds. We've become the substitute for prehistoric sloths.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Getting others to help often requires giving them something they want. Fruit teaches that the best partnerships are mutually beneficial. You get transported; they get fed. Everybody wins.

outro.script: That's Day 146. Tomorrow, we'll explore what counts as a vegetable. Until then, when you eat fruit, remember: you're being bribed by a plant.

growTrack.title: Mutual Benefit - Create Win-Wins
growTrack.activity: Think of a relationship where both sides benefit—a 'fruit deal' in your life. Where are you providing value to get something you need? Where might you create new mutual benefits? The best partnerships make both sides better off.
